7 questions on the same ideas, drawn from this exercise's answer key. These are auto-graded and reported.
Week 1: the team voted in a group chat and started coding that afternoon, reasoning ""we know what students want, we ARE students."" Which phase did they skip?

column2: a group-chat vote is a valid investigation</button>

column1: Correct. Investigating and reflecting is where requirements get determined. Voting among themselves determined nothing about future users.
Incorrect. Testing does fail later, in Week 4, and it fails in a more interesting way: they tested and then ignored the result.
Incorrect. A vote records preferences the team already held. It collects no data from the people who will use the program.
Incorrect. Design was skipped too, but not in Week 1. The sketch arrives in Week 3, and its problem is timing rather than absence.
What would have replaced the team's ""we ARE students"" assumption with something defensible?
Incorrect. More voters inside the same team is a larger sample of exactly the same assumption.
Incorrect. Studying competitors can inform a design, but it is not one of the methods the CED names, and it still never contacts a user.
Incorrect. Prototyping belongs to a later phase and cannot supply the requirements the prototype is meant to satisfy.
Correct. These are the CED's named investigation methods. Each one puts data from users where the team had only beliefs about users.
Week 2: the team built login, decks, quiz mode, streaks and sharing in one push, planning to ""test at the end."" Which development approach did they reject, and what is it?
Incorrect. Iteration is a different failure, and the team commits it separately in Week 4. Iteration is about responding to feedback, not about build order.
Incorrect. The work was in fact divided badly, but collaboration is not the approach this week's decision rejected.
Correct. Five separately confirmed pieces would have replaced one 900 line unknown. That verification step is the definition.
Incorrect. Agile is not the vocabulary the CED uses here, and naming it would not earn the point.
Week 3: the team drew a paper sketch of all the screens after the code was already written and called it ""our design doc."" What is wrong with the timing?

column2: documenting the finished screens is a legitimate design record</button>

column1: Incorrect. The medium is irrelevant. A paper storyboard drawn in Week 1 would have done the job perfectly.
Correct. Design is forward looking by definition. Worse here, no investigation ever happened, so there was no specification for a design to accomplish.
Incorrect. Approval is not what the design phase is for, and the teacher request is why the sketch exists at all.
Incorrect. A drawing of what already exists is a portrait, not a blueprint. It cannot guide a build that is finished.
Week 4: four of five testers could not find the quiz button. The team logged this and changed nothing, saying ""they are just not good with apps."" What did an iterative process require here?
Correct. Iteration is the willingness to let test results send you backward. The layout, not the testers, was the thing to revise.
Incorrect. The testing phase did run. What failed is the loop that makes testing worth anything.
Incorrect. A tutorial explaining an unfindable button treats the symptom and leaves the design defect in place.
Incorrect. Replacing the testers discards the finding. The feedback was consistent, which is what makes it a requirement discovery.
Week 5: a streak-counter segment was pasted from a coding forum and its variables renamed. What does the CED require?
Incorrect. A spoken mention is not the program documentation, and it does not travel with the code.
Incorrect. Renaming variables changes the spelling, not the source. This is the exact reasoning the case exists to reject.
Incorrect. Borrowed code is allowed. The requirement is acknowledgement, not abstinence.
Correct. A comment above the streak counter naming the forum satisfies both halves: it lives in the documentation and it names the origin.
Week 6: one member added comments to all 900 lines the night before the demo, from memory. Why is this still a documentation failure?
Incorrect. The volume is a symptom. Even 90 lines reconstructed from memory at the end would fail the same way.
Incorrect. Comments are documentation. The problem is when they were written, not what form they took.
Correct. Documentation written after development is over cannot catch wrong assumptions or let teammates build on each other's work. Those jobs were already lost.
Incorrect. Solo documentation is permitted. The CED describes documenting individually or collaboratively.

6 questions on the same ideas, drawn from this exercise's answer key. These are auto-graded and reported.
Scenario 1: a locker-organizer app assumes lockers are assigned alphabetically, but this school assigns them by grade and hallway. No teacher was consulted. Which process problem is this?
<div id=""chk-1-fb-A"" class=""mcq-feedback incorrect-fb"">Incorrect. Nothing in the scenario says pieces went unverified. The month of building may have gone fine
column2: it went toward the wrong target.

column1: Correct. Investigation is the CED's named tool for replacing beliefs about users with data from users. It never ran.
Incorrect. Writing the wrong assumption down more clearly would not have made it right.
Incorrect. The code does what it was designed to do. This is a correct build of the wrong program, not a defect in the build.
Scenario 1, second layer: what follows from the fact that requirements were never determined?
Correct. Requirements feed the specification, and the specification is what design exists to accomplish. Losing the first collapses the chain.
Incorrect. Requirements written now can guide future work, but they cannot retroactively justify the month already spent.
Incorrect. A missing investigation propagates. Design had nothing to design toward.
Incorrect. ""Every planned feature"" begs the question, since the plan itself was guessed. Done was undefined from day one.

Scenario 2: one partner wrote a 700-line escape-room game in four days, ran it for the first time, and after a week of fixes cannot say which parts have ever worked. Which sentence gives the diagnosis away?
Incorrect. Team size is not the issue. One partner building alone incrementally would have avoided this.
Incorrect. Length alone is not a process problem. A 700-line program built in verified pieces would be fine.
Incorrect. An instant crash is a symptom shared by many causes and does not by itself name the process disease.
Correct. Incremental development confirms each piece at the moment it joins, so that sentence could never be true.
Scenario 2, second layer: the pair's testing strategy was ""run it once at the end."" Where should a testing strategy have been developed?
Incorrect. Investigation determines requirements. Those requirements later supply expected outcomes, but the strategy itself is a design product.
Incorrect. A strategy written after the failure cannot have prevented it, and the pair are still guessing which pieces work.
Correct. The CED places the testing strategy inside design, which is why a project that skips design usually discovers it has no strategy either.
Incorrect. Deciding how to test at the moment of testing is what produced ""run it once at the end.""

Scenario 3: users tap the poster image expecting a button. The team logs every comment and ships unchanged, because ""the design phase ended in October and we are in the testing phase now."" What is wrong with that reasoning?

column2: phases must be completed in order to keep a project on schedule</button>

column1: Incorrect. They did log every comment. Collecting feedback and then discarding it is exactly the failure.
Correct. Revisiting earlier phases is part of what iteration means, so ""we are past design"" misreads the process model itself.
Incorrect. These were the first real users. Their confusion is a requirements discovery, not a sampling error.
Incorrect. This is the misreading the scenario is built on. A phase label cannot veto a revision the process definition requires.
Scenario 4: a student in a block-based environment with no comment feature keeps no documentation at all, calling it ""not possible in this language."" Rule on the excuse.
Correct. A written design log describing each procedure's function and history is the other method the CED calls for.
Incorrect. A verbal explanation is not a written description of function and development, and it does not persist.
Incorrect. The Create PT requirement exists, but the documentation rule stands on its own regardless of the task.
Incorrect. The CED anticipates exactly this environment and answers it directly. No comment support never becomes no documentation needed.
